source: Jaroslawicz, Whiting, Shah, Maamari (2025) How Many Instructions Can LLMs Follow at Once? (IFScale)
finding: 20 models, 10 to 500 keyword-inclusion instructions in a business-report task. Best models reach only about 68% at 500. Three decay shapes: threshold (reasoning models), linear, exponential.
numbers: Abstract: best frontier model about 68% at 500. Text: o3 62.8%, grok-3 61.9%, claude-3.7-sonnet 52.7%, claude-opus-4 44.6%, claude-sonnet-4 42.9%, deepseek-r1 30.9%, qwen3 26.9% at 500. The appendix table is garbled in text extraction; a row ending 98.4/84.8/68.9 sitting next to gemini-2.5-pro suggests gemini-2.5-pro is the 68% model, but this is inferred, not read cleanly. Results averaged over 5 runs.
quote: even the best frontier models only achieve 68% accuracy at the max density of 500 instructions
limits: Only keyword inclusion (a simple rule type); one task. Claude thinking on/off is shown only in a figure; text says moderate gains at high densities, no numbers.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 7 in part: top model was most likely gemini-2.5-pro, not o3. Rule holding is a loss curve, not a fixed cap; reasoning models hold near 100% to about 100-250 rules.

source: Jaroslawicz et al. (2025) IFScale, degradation shapes and primacy
finding: Reasoning models show threshold decay: near-perfect until a critical density, then rising variance. Non-reasoning models decay linearly or exponentially. Early instructions are favoured at mid density; at 300+ rules failure becomes uniform.
numbers: Primacy effect (error ratio last third to first third) peaks near 150-200 instructions, then falls toward 1.0-1.5 beyond 300. Omission to modification error ratio rises with density (claude-3.5-haiku row: 0.00 at 10 up to 31.69 at 500). Reasoning-model latency grows (one model 12.4 s at 10 to 436 s at 250).
limits: Omission errors dominate at high load: the model drops rules rather than misapplying them.
agent_relevance: Supports a rule register checked item by item: at high load the failure is omission, so a checklist pass targets the right error. Put the most important rules first.

source: Cook, Rocktaschel, Foerster, Aumiller, Wang (2024) Ticking All the Boxes: Generated Checklists Improve LLM Evaluation and Generation (TICK/STICK)
finding: A generated YES/NO checklist, used as the critique in one refinement pass, improves answers. Unstructured self-critique (Self-Refine) often hurts.
numbers: Abstract: LiveBench reasoning +7.8 abs with STICK. Table 1 overall: STICK +3.8 for Command-R+, +0.8 for GPT-4o, while Self-Refine degraded both (GPT-4o Instructions 50.4 to 36.4 with Self-Refine, 51.6 with STICK). InFoBench +6.5, WildBench +7.1 (Command-R+). Best-of-N by STICK: +5.1 InFoBench, +5.3 WildBench.
limits: Extra calls and tokens are spent, so not an equal-token test. Gains small for the strongest model (GPT-4o +0.8).
agent_relevance: Direct test of a checklist re-pass: helps weak and mid models, adds little for strong ones, and free-form self-critique can make things worse. Use item-wise YES/NO checks, not a generic review.

source: Hersche, Camposampiero, Wattenhofer, Sebastian, Rahimi (2024) Towards Learning to Reason: Comparing LLMs with Neuro-Symbolic on Arithmetic Relations in Abstract Reasoning (I-RAVEN-X)
finding: Text-form RAVEN with oracle perception. GPT-4 and Llama-3 70B do well on constant, progression, distribute-three rules but fail arithmetic. I-RAVEN-X widens the grid (3x10) and the value range (50, 100, 1000).
numbers: I-RAVEN 3x3: GPT-4 93.2%, Llama-3 70B 85.0%. I-RAVEN-X 3x10 at range 50/100/1000: GPT-4 82.2/79.6/76.6, Llama 76.8/73.0/74.2. Arithmetic-rule accuracy: GPT-4 73.6 on 3x3 then 30.4/25.1/8.4; Llama 45.0 then 1.5/2.6/0.4. Table IV: arithmetic 27.1% for GPT-4 without per-attribute queries, 73.6% with them. Neuro-symbolic ARLC (programmed) 99.7-100%.
limits: Varies grid length and value range, NOT the number of rules per item. So it does not test the Carpenter 1990 rule-count prediction. Old models (GPT-4-0613, Llama-3).
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partly: collapse follows operation type (arithmetic) and number size, not rule count. One query per attribute lifted GPT-4 arithmetic from 27% to 74%: a chunking effect, like the human WM story.

source: Camposampiero et al. (2025) Can Large Reasoning Models do Analogical Reasoning under Perceptual Uncertainty? (full table re-read)
finding: Re-reading Table 1 and text corrects how the I-RAVEN-X collapse should be read: the big drop comes from simulated perceptual noise (confounders plus smoothed distributions), not from longer rows or wider ranges.
numbers: Clean I-RAVEN range 10 to I-RAVEN-X range 1000 (3x10): o3-mini medium 86.6 to 81.0 (5.6 pt loss), R1 80.6 to 82.8 (gain 2.2); o3-mini tokens 5445 to 7209. Only with both noise types at max: o3-mini 17.0%, R1 22.8% (chance 12.5%). High effort o3-mini: 92.6 on I-RAVEN but 80.6 at range 1000 (2.7x tokens, no gain). Max noise high effort: 31.0% with 53,596 tokens.
limits: Earlier evidence line c24 quoted 86.6 to 17.0 as longer matrices and wider ranges. That mixes in the noise. c24 gave R1 23.2; text says 22.8.
agent_relevance: Correction for claim K19. Reasoning models do not collapse on longer rows or wider ranges; they collapse when the given facts are uncertain. Uncertain inputs need a verified state, not more thinking.

source: Shojaee, Mirzadeh, Alizadeh, Horton, Bengio, Farajtabar (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: On controllable puzzles, thinking models beat non-thinking at medium size, then all collapse to zero at a model-specific size. Giving the exact solution algorithm in the prompt did not move the collapse point.
numbers: Tower of Hanoi collapse around N=7-8 disks (100-200 moves); first error near move 40 for N=8 (255 moves) and within the first 100 moves for N=10; up to about 100 correct moves in Hanoi but only 4 in River Crossing. Algorithm given: performance does not improve (Fig 8, Hanoi and Checker Jumping). Temperature 0 vs sampling: no change in collapse (R1 Blocks World collapse N=4 at T=0, N=30 with sampling).
limits: Published critiques argue some failures are output-length artifacts or unsolvable instances (not opened here). The authors appendix argues failures occur well inside context limits.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: execution of a known procedure fails at a length threshold even with the rules fully given. Rule following needs checkpointed state and re-verification, not just a rule list.

source: Meyerson et al. (2025) Solving a Million-Step LLM Task with Zero Errors (MAKER)
finding: Tower of Hanoi with 20 disks (1,048,575 steps) solved with zero errors by extreme decomposition: each microagent gets the current state, makes one move, returns the next state; first-ahead-by-k voting and red-flagging fix errors.
numbers: Per-step error rate stays stable as disks grow. Per-step error estimates: gpt-4.1-nano about 0.357 (not viable), gpt-4.1-mini about 0.0045, o3-mini about 0.0017. Table cost estimate for gpt-4.1-mini about 3.5K dollars for the full task.
limits: Explicit external state passed at every step, plus voting and many calls, so not an equal-token comparison with a single pass. Cheap models suffice; big reasoning models not required.
agent_relevance: Closest direct evidence for gap 1: writing the full state out each step removes the length collapse seen in single runs. Rule-count scaling was not tested.

source: Zhang, Jian, Ouyang, Vosoughi (2024) Working Memory Identifies Reasoning Limits in Language Models (EMNLP 2024)
finding: N-back on GPT-family models, then cognitive-science prompt fixes (chunking, rehearsal, attention cues) applied to BBH tasks. Restating the state in compact chunks raised accuracy on state-tracking tasks.
numbers: Tracking Shuffled Objects, text-davinci-002: chunked name(color)-swap status-list prompt reached 96.4%, +35.4 points over the original CoT prompt. Web of Lies with code-style prompt 96.4% (+4.8). Temporal Sequence, GPT-3.5: a re-check cue lifted accuracy to 96% (+32.8). text-ada-001 with a short cue 25.4% (+15.8). Human n-back d-prime 3.39-4.05 (4x4 grid); small LMs 0.01-2.51.
limits: Old models (2022-23). Prompt rewrites also change tokens and format, so not a clean capacity test. Authors made the fixes by hand after failure analysis.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 1: a rewritten running state (status list) lifts state-tracking accuracy a lot. No test of gain vs rule count and no equal-token control.

source: Xiong, Ji-An, Huang, Wilson, Lee, Wei (2026) In-context superposition: human-like working memory interference in LLMs (COLM 2026), re-read for gap 3
finding: Across 10 open models in non-thinking mode, mean N-back accuracy correlates with MMLU-Pro, GPQA Diamond and IFEval; log parameter count does not significantly predict any of them.
numbers: Autoregressive r: MMLU-Pro .78, GPQA Diamond .88, IFEval .69. Teacher forcing: .70, .72, .82. Lure condition vs accuracy r -.51 (autoregressive), -.32 (teacher forced). Authors cite human r = .31-.78.
limits: N = 10 models, so r has wide error. Benchmarks are knowledge, graduate science and instruction following, not matrix reasoning. Thinking mode disabled. No partial correlation controlling for size read. Better-trained models are better at everything (positive manifold).
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays mostly open: an LLM WM-reasoning link exists but is confounded by general quality; no matrix-reasoning or thinking-mode test.

source: Melby-Lervag, Redick, Hulme (2016) WM training meta-analysis, reopened for control type and N-back
finding: Control type is the key moderator for nonverbal ability. N-back with active controls shows a small gain that comes from a few small, single-test, crossover studies. WM gains did not predict gains in nonverbal ability.
numbers: Passive vs treated controls on nonverbal ability: Q(1)=6.09, p=.01. N-back with treated controls g=0.15, p=.02, driven by the five largest effects: all under 20 per group, one nonverbal test, and 4 of 5 with control-group pre-to-post drops larger than training gains. Meta-regression: control type beta=.27, p=.04; gain on trained-type WM tasks vs nonverbal gain beta=-.01, p=.86, k=26. Visuospatial WM gain vs nonverbal gain beta=.13, p=.10, k=38. Follow-up about 5 months: no nonverbal effect with treated controls.
limits: Authors criticise Au 2014 for ignoring baseline differences; the critique is theirs, not independent.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 6: the 0.05 vs 0.24 gap is explained by control type, baseline correction, n-back only vs all programmes, and adults only. WM gains did not mediate Gf gains, so more capacity giving more reasoning fails as a causal rule.

source: Melby-Lervag and Hulme (2016) There is no convincing evidence that working memory training is effective: a reply to Au et al. (2014) and Karbach and Verhaeghen (2014), as cited in the 2016 meta-analysis
finding: Reply paper, not opened. The argument as stated in the opened 2016 meta-analysis: Au 2014 and Karbach 2014 used posttest-only differences with no baseline adjustment, covered only n-back and ages 18-50 (Au), and fewer studies.
numbers: No figures from the reply itself.

source: Au, Sheehan, Tsai, Duncan, Buschkuehl, Jaeggi (2015) Improving fluid intelligence with training on working memory: a meta-analysis (Psychon Bull Rev)
finding: Abstract read on PubMed. N-back only, 20 studies, healthy adults 18-50 with a control group; small but significant positive effect on Gf.
numbers: 20 studies (abstract). The headline g = 0.24 and the active-control split were not retrievable (paywalled); not claimed here.
limits: Abstract only. Scope differs from Melby-Lervag (all programmes, all ages, 87 papers).
agent_relevance: Gap 6: scope and method differences, not just noise, explain the disagreement. Stays contested for n-back in adults.

source: Burgoyne and Engle (2020) Attention Control: A Cornerstone of Higher-Order Cognition (Curr Dir Psychol Sci)
finding: Abstract read via Crossref. Attention control (maintenance and disengagement) is the common thread among Gf, WMC and sensory discrimination. New attention-control tasks have higher reliability, stronger intercorrelations and higher loadings on a common factor than older tasks.
limits: Abstract only. The restraint vs constraint wording in the critique list could not be tied to this paper or to Kane 2016 from what was read.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: human work separates holding from disengaging; no LLM study separates them.

source: Lee and Engle (2026, preprint) The Primacy of Fluid Intelligence in Hypothesis Sampling: Not Working Memory and Beyond Attention Control
finding: Large community sample, latent-variable SEM. Avoiding re-testing rejected hypotheses is predicted by Gf, which fully absorbs the effect of WMC. Attention control does not mediate; only selective attention predicts resampling.
numbers: Abstract only; no N or coefficients read.
agent_relevance: Gaps 9 and 1: not re-testing rejected options depends on disengaging from them (Gf, selective attention), not on holding more. Suggests an explicit rejected list in the S-state.

source: Kane et al. (2016) Individual differences in the executive control of attention, memory, and thought, and their associations with schizotypy (J Exp Psychol Gen)
finding: Located by Crossref (DOI 10.1037/xge0000184), no abstract returned. Not opened.
limits: Cannot confirm what it says about restraint vs constraint.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 remains unverified for this source.

source: Open-access connectome study (N=297) comparing localist theories with Process Overlap Theory (Kovacs and Conway 2016), PMC9921238
finding: Global whole-brain connectivity predicts general intelligence better than localised accounts; POT and Network Neuroscience Theory are the global accounts. POT is described as overlap of multiple networks engaged by task demands.
quote: functional overlap among multiple brain regions and networks that are selectively engaged on the basis of task demands
limits: Human neuroimaging only. No LLM study tests POT. LLM prediction here is my inference: a shared bottleneck predicts one capacity-load curve across tasks; POT predicts many task-specific limits whose overlap makes a g-like factor.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: no distinct LLM test exists. A scaffold test would be cross-task: if one load manipulation hurts all rule tasks equally it is a bottleneck; if hits are task-specific it is overlap.

source: Adapala (2025) Cognitive Load Limits in Large Language Models: Benchmarking Multi-Hop Reasoning (ICE)
finding: Interleaved Cognitive Evaluation: extraneous context (saturation) and task switching (residue) on multi-hop questions. 200 questions, 10 replications each, five instruction-tuned models.
numbers: Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2: 0% in all conditions including control. Gemini-2.0-Flash-001: 85% in control, slope -0.003 per percent load, p<0.001.
limits: Single author, preprint, small slope, weak old models, floor effect for small models.
agent_relevance: Weak support that irrelevant context load lowers multi-hop reasoning. Not a capacity-versus-reasoning test.
